brief: Quick Connect: Initiate is anonymous, so live codes can be flooded. Options: (A) a fixed maximum of live codes, refusing new Initiate past it; (B) evict the oldest live code; (C) per-address Initiate caps beside a global cap, needing trustedProxies; (D) no cap.
tradeoff: Under a flood, either a new TV cannot start Quick Connect until codes expire (A), or a TV already showing a code has it silently stop working (B). With no cap, live codes fill the 6-digit space, so a viewer's mistyped approval can sign a stranger's device into their account.
entry: Option A: at most 100 live codes across all replicas, pending or approved and unredeemed; past it Initiate is refused and no code already issued is touched, so a code a TV shows works for its full time. Not configurable. 100 is far above the devices a deployment of hundreds of viewers pairs within 10 minutes, and when full of a flooder's codes a mistyped approval lands on one about 1 time in 10,000. Each refused Initiate is logged with its reason and counted in a metric; docs/access.md and docs/running.md state the cap and that password sign-in is unaffected. The refusal's status is chosen from what jellyfin-web is observed to show for it, so that it does not read as an unreachable server. Rejected: B (an honest viewer's approval then fails as an unknown code and counts toward D-078's bound, so a flood would lock honest accounts out; the failure arrives late and unexplained); D (the mistyped-approval risk above). Backlog: C, promoted when the metric shows the cap reached on the dogfood or at an operator's. Given up: an anonymous flooder can keep new TVs from starting Quick Connect while the flood lasts, and together with name guessing (D-020) can keep a viewer on a new device out; known devices and password sign-in still work.
serves: PRODUCT.md: 'Signing in is easy and safe'; 'Failure modes are designed, tested and reported. Nothing fails silently'; 'Operating it stays boring'.
